edition.locus: Divine Institutes 6.25 (donum integritas / sacrificium laus / templum in pectore)

source_text: Nunc de sacrificio ipso pauca dicamus. ebur inquit Plato non castum donum deo. quid ergo? picta scilicet et texta pretiosa? immo uero non castum donum deo quidquid corrumpi, quidquid subripi potest. sed sicut hoc uidit, non oportere uiuenti offerri aliquid quod sit ex mortuo corpore, cur illud non uidit, non debere incorporali corporale munus offerri? quanto melius et uerius Seneca uultisne uos inquit deum cogitare magnum et placidum et maiestate leni uerendum, amicum et semper in proximo, non immo lationibus nec sanguine multo colendum — quae enim ei trucidatione immerentium uoluptas est? —, sed mente pura, bono honestoque proposito? non templa illi congestis in altitudinem saxis extruenda sunt: in suo cuique consecrandus est pectore. uestes igitur et gemmas et cetera quae habentur in pretio si quis putat deo cara, is plane quid sit deus nescit: cui putat uoluptati esse eas res quas etiam homo si contempserit, iure laudabitur. quid ergo castum, quid deo dignum nisi quod ipse in illa diuina lege sua poposcit? duo sunt quae offerri debeant, donum et sacrificium, donum in perpetuum, sacrificium ad tempus. uerum apud istos, qui nullo modo rationem diuinitatis intellegunt, donum est quidquid auro argentoque fabricatur, item quidquid purpura et serico texitur, sacrificiumque uictima et quaecumque in ara cremantur. sed utroque non utitur deus, quia et ipse incorruptus est et illud totum corruptibile. itaque deo utrumque incorporale offerendum est, quo utitur. donum est integritas animi, sacrificium laus et hymnus; si enim deus non uidetur, ergo his rebus coli debet quae non uidentur. nulla igitur alia religio uera est nisi quae uirtute et iustitia constat. quomodo autem deus iustitia hominis utatur, intellectu facile est. si enim iustus fuerit homo, accepta immortalitate in aeternum deo seruiet. omnes autem non nisi ad iustitiam nasci cum philosophi ueteres tum etiam Cicero suspicatur. disserens enim de legibus sed omnium inquit quae in hominum doctorum disputatione uersantur, nihil est profecto praestabilius quam plane intellegi nos ad iustitiam esse natos. id ergo solum deo exhibere atque offerre debemus ad quod capiendum nos ipse generauit. hoc autem duplex sacrificii genus quam sit uerissimum, Trismegistus Hermes idoneus testis est, qui nobiscum, id est cum prophetis quos sequimur, tam re quam uerbis congruit. de iustitia sic locutus est: hoc uerbum, o fili, adora et cole. cultus autem dei unus est malum non esse. item in illo sermone perfecto, cum exaudisset Asclepium quaerentem a filio suo utrum placeret patri eius proferri tus et alios odores ad sacrificium dei, exclamauit: bene, bene ominare, o Asclepi. est enim maxima inpietas tale quid de uno illo ac singulari bono in animum inducere. haec et his similia huic non conueniunt: omnium enim quaecumque sunt plenus est et omnium minime indigens. nos uero gratias agentes adoremus: huius enim sacrificium sola benedictio est. et recte. uerbo enim sacrificari oportet deo, siquidem deus uerbum est, ut ipse confessus est. summus igitur colendi dei ritus est ex ore iusti hominis ad deum directa laudatio, quae tamen ipsa ut deo sit accepta, et humilitate et timore et deuotione maxima opus est, ne quis forte integritatis atque innocentiae fiduciam gerens tumoris et adrogantiae crimen incurrat eoque facto gratiam uirtutis amittat. sed ut sit deo carus omnique macula careat, misericordiam dei semper inploret nihilque aliut precetur nisi peccatis suis ueniam, licet nulla sint. si quid ahut desiderauerit, non est opus dicto scienti quid uelimus: si quid ei boni euenerit, gratias agat, si quid mali, satisfaciat et id sibi ob peccata sua euenisse fateatur. et nihilo minus etiam in malis gratias agat et in bonis satisfaciat, ut idem sit semper et stabilis et immutabilis et inconcussus. nec tantum hoc in templo putet sibi esse faciendum, sed et domi et in ipso etiam cubili suo. secum denique habeat deum semper in corde suo consecratum, quoniam ipse est dei templum. quodsi deo, patri ac domino, hac adsiduitate, hoc obsequio, hac deuotione seruierit, consummata et perfecta iustitia est: quam qui tenuerit, hic, ut ante testati sumus, deo paruit, hic religioni atque officio suo satisfecit.
pass_a_gloss: Plato saw ivory is no pure gift for God — nor painted or woven treasures, nor anything that can rot or be stolen — yet missed that an incorporeal God must not be offered a bodily gift. Seneca spoke better: God is great, calm, near, not to be worshiped with blood but with a pure mind and honest purpose; each must consecrate God in his own breast. What is pure and worthy of God except what he asked in his divine law? Two things must be offered: gift forever, sacrifice for a time — both incorporeal: gift is integrity of mind, sacrifice is praise and hymn. No other religion is true except what stands by virtue and justice; the just human, receiving immortality, serves God forever. Hermes agrees: worship of God is one — not to be evil; his sacrifice is blessing alone. Highest rite is praise from a just mouth directed to God — with humility, fear, devotion — always begging mercy and pardon even when there seem no sins. Keep God consecrated in the heart: that is God's temple. Serve the Father and Lord with that constancy, obedience, devotion: then justice is complete, and religion and duty are satisfied.
pass_b_english: Now let us say a few things about the sacrifice itself. Ivory, says Plato, is not a pure gift for God. What then? Painted things and precious weavings? On the contrary, whatever can be corrupted, whatever can be stolen, is not a pure gift for God. But as he saw that something from a dead body ought not to be offered to the living, why did he not see that a bodily gift ought not to be offered to the incorporeal? How much better and truer is Seneca: Do you want, he says, to think of God as great and calm and to be revered with gentle majesty, a friend and always near, to be worshiped not with slaughtered victims nor with much blood — for what pleasure is there for him in the slaughter of the undeserving? — but with a pure mind and a good and honest purpose? Temples need not be built for him with stones piled high: he is to be consecrated in each person's breast. Therefore if anyone thinks clothes and gems and the other things held precious are dear to God, he plainly does not know what God is: he thinks those things are a pleasure to him which even a human, if he has despised them, will be rightly praised. What then is pure, what worthy of God, except what he himself demanded in that divine law of his?

There are two things that ought to be offered, gift and sacrifice — gift forever, sacrifice for a time. But among those who in no way understand the account of divinity, gift is whatever is fashioned from gold and silver, likewise whatever is woven from purple and silk, and sacrifice is the victim and whatever is burned on the altar. But God uses neither, because he himself is incorrupt and that whole thing is corruptible. And so both must be offered to God incorporeal, which he uses. Gift is integrity of mind; sacrifice is praise and hymn. For if God is not seen, he ought therefore to be worshiped with those things that are not seen. No other religion is therefore true except that which consists in virtue and justice. But how God uses a human's justice is easy to understand. For if a human has been just, having received immortality he will serve God forever. But that all are born for nothing except justice both the ancient philosophers and also Cicero suspect. For discoursing on the laws he says: but of all things that turn in the dispute of learned humans, nothing is surely more excellent than that it be plainly understood we were born for justice. That alone therefore we ought to present and offer to God for the taking of which he himself generated us. But how most true this twofold kind of sacrifice is, Hermes Trismegistus is a fit witness, who agrees with us — that is, with the prophets we follow — as much in substance as in words. Of justice he spoke thus: This word, O son, adore and worship. But the worship of God is one: not to be evil. Likewise in that perfect discourse, when he had heard Asclepius asking his son whether it pleased his father that incense and other scents be brought out for God's sacrifice, he cried out: Speak well, speak well, O Asclepius. For it is the greatest impiety to bring such a thing about that one and singular Good into the mind. These and things like them do not suit him: for he is full of all things whatever are and least in need of all. But let us adore giving thanks: for his sacrifice is blessing alone. And rightly. For one ought to sacrifice to God by word, since indeed God is the Word, as he himself confessed.

The highest rite of worshiping God therefore is praise directed to God from the mouth of a just human, which yet, that it may be acceptable to God, needs both humility and fear and the greatest devotion, lest anyone perhaps carrying confidence of integrity and innocence run into the charge of swelling and arrogance and by that act lose the grace of virtue. But that he may be dear to God and free from every stain, let him always implore God's mercy and pray for nothing else than pardon for his sins, even if there are none. If he has desired anything else, there is no need of speech to the one who knows what we want: if any good has come to him, let him give thanks; if any evil, let him make satisfaction and confess that it happened to him because of his sins. And nonetheless even in evils let him give thanks and in goods make satisfaction, so that he may always be the same and stable and unchangeable and unshaken. And let him think this must be done for himself not only in the temple, but also at home and even in his own bedroom. Finally let him always have God with him, consecrated in his heart, since he himself is God's temple. But if he has served God, the Father and Lord, with this constancy, this obedience, this devotion, justice is consummated and perfect: which whoever has held, this one, as we testified before, has obeyed God, this one has satisfied religion and his duty.

lemmas.gloss: gift to God = integrity of mind (incorporeal)
sacrifice = praise and hymn, not blood
consecrate God in the breast; human is God's temple
Hermes: one worship of God — not to be evil

rejected: gold, purple, incense, and bloody victims as God's gifts
choices.why: God is incorporeal and needs nothing corruptible; gift is integrity, sacrifice is praise.

rejected: stone temples and piled altars as the true house of God
choices.why: Seneca and Lactantius: consecrate God in the breast; the human is God's temple.
Highest praise needs humility and fear; always ask pardon lest arrogance lose virtue's grace.
